name: Virga
desc: Rain that never lands — shafts hang out of a ragged cloud base, get raked sideways by the wind shear into the classic scythe hook, and evaporate into a frayed nothing partway down, so the scene beneath stays perfectly dry; shafts are born, reach, tatter and die on their own clocks while the base drifts and mammates overhead and a low sun wanders behind the whole curtain and lights it from within.

energy.doc: storm force — shaft opacity and fall rate, cloud-base density, how hard the wind shears the shafts over

scale.doc: shaft width vs design size — 2.0 merges them into one continuous curtain

density.doc: how many shafts are alive at once (3–18) + fall-streak count

shear.doc: wind shear — how far the shafts hook downwind, and which way (negative hooks left)

reach.doc: how far down the shafts get before they evaporate — 0 kills them right under the base, 1 almost lets them land

hue.doc: primary hue — leaden blue by default; the style ramps swing off it

x.doc: where the light sits behind the base

y.doc: cloud-base height as a canvas fraction — everything hangs from here

style.doc: aesthetic — overcast: cold documentary grey-blue under a leaden base · sunset: violet base with shafts burning gold from the low sun behind · dust: dry ochre microburst virga over desert · radar: reflectivity false-colour quantised into hard dBZ bands with range rings and azimuth spokes, an instrument readout rather than a sky · engraving: the whole field resolved into ruled hatch lines, a meteorological plate

act.doc: multi-minute programme — drift: a steady parade of shafts crossing · microburst: shafts periodically surge down hard and reach much further · dissipate: the base thins out and the shafts shorten and go rare over minutes, then rebuild
